local.levelRationale: Citywide annual-average PM2.5 (~6.65 µg/m³, 2024) is roughly 33% above the WHO 2021 Air Quality Guideline of 5 µg/m³ but comfortably meets the US EPA annual NAAQS of 9.0 µg/m³ (revised Feb 2024). Scored primarily against the WHO guideline per research brief instruction; NYC is 'needs attention, mild' against the health-protective benchmark while formally 'attaining' the weaker federal standard.
local.indicator: NYCCAS annual average fine particulate matter (PM2.5)
local.value: ~6.65 µg/m³ citywide (author-computed unweighted mean across all 59 community districts); individual community districts range from 5.3 µg/m³ (Rockaway and Broad Channel, Queens CD14) to 10.5 µg/m³ (Midtown, Manhattan CD5). Citywide PM2.5 has declined 29-36% since 2009 depending on the report vintage cited by DOHMH.
local.target: WHO 2021 Air Quality Guideline: 5 µg/m³ annual PM2.5 (primary scoring target per research brief). Secondary/regulatory target: US EPA NAAQS, revised Feb 7, 2024 from 12 to 9.0 µg/m³ annual (NYC attains this).
local.geographicScale: city (computed by aggregating DOHMH's official community-district-level data — see dataGaps; DOHMH does not appear to publish one single 'citywide' PM2.5 headline number in its public materials)
local.context: NYC's PM2.5 story is fundamentally about intra-city gradient, not a single citywide number: the ~2x range from Rockaway (Queens, 5.3 µg/m³) to Midtown (Manhattan, 10.5 µg/m³) reflects traffic density, building-heating combustion, and street-canyon effects, not a uniform exposure. NYCCAS is a ~100-site seasonal monitoring network run by DOHMH and Queens College (CUNY) covering all 59 community districts since 2009 — one of the most granular urban air-monitoring systems in the US. Local Law 43 (2010) and the NYC Clean Heat program are the biggest documented policy win, having eliminated No. 6 heating oil citywide by 2015 and cut PM2.5 emissions from heating by an estimated 65%. Wildfire smoke (see subIndicators) is now a major confounder that DOHMH itself flags as disrupting the underlying downward trend. Congestion pricing (since Jan 2025) is independently measured to be reducing PM2.5 in and near the Manhattan CBD.
local.source: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH), NYC Community Air Survey (NYCCAS), Appendix 3: Community District Average Pollutant Levels
local.productionVsConsumption: production-based (locally emitted — traffic, building combustion, construction, some regional/transboundary contribution noted in global lens)

queens.value: 6.07 µg/m³ (author-computed unweighted mean of Queens's 14 community districts, 2024)

statenIsland.value: 6.00 µg/m³ (author-computed unweighted mean of Staten Island's 3 community districts, 2024) — lowest of the five boroughs

local.neighborhoodNote: Highest 2024 PM2.5: Midtown, Manhattan (Community District 5), 10.5 µg/m³. Lowest: Rockaway and Broad Channel, Queens (Community District 14), 5.3 µg/m³ — roughly a 2x intra-city gradient. On health burden rather than raw concentration, the sharpest disparity is asthma: Hunts Point-Mott Haven (South Bronx) had a child (ages 5-17) asthma ED visit rate of 266.2 per 10,000 in 2023 versus 143.7 per 10,000 citywide (NYC Environment & Health Data Portal neighborhood report). An older but more geographically complete DOHMH dataset (2016) found Hunts Point-Mott Haven at 502.7 per 10,000 and neighboring East Harlem at 578.4 per 10,000, both roughly 20x the rate in low-poverty Bayside-Little Neck, Queens (22.4 per 10,000) — DOHMH Epi Data Brief No. 126.

subIndicators.name: NO2 annual average, highest/lowest community districts
subIndicators.value: Citywide NO2 declined 38-41% since 2009 (DOHMH). 2024 community-district range: 25.1 ppb (Midtown, Manhattan CD5, highest) to 4.8 ppb (Rockaway and Broad Channel, Queens CD14, lowest)

subIndicators.name: Summertime average ozone (NYCCAS descriptive metric, not the EPA regulatory design value)
subIndicators.value: 2024 community-district range: 27.1 ppb (Midtown, Manhattan CD5, lowest — consistent with NOx titration suppressing ozone in the densest traffic core) to 38.4 ppb (Rockaway and Broad Channel, Queens CD14, highest — coastal/outer-borough areas see more regional ozone transport)

subIndicators.name: NY-NJ-CT 8-hour ozone nonattainment classification
subIndicators.value: Reclassified from 'Moderate' to 'Serious' nonattainment for the 2015 ozone NAAQS (70 ppb) after the area missed its August 3, 2024 attainment deadline
subIndicators.source: US EPA, Federal Register final rule

subIndicators.name: PM2.5-attributable deaths
subIndicators.value: ~2,000 excess deaths per year from cardiovascular/respiratory disease attributable to long-term PM2.5 exposure — about 1 in every 25 deaths citywide
subIndicators.source: NYC DOHMH, cited in NYC Health press release on NYCCAS congestion-pricing evaluation

subIndicators.name: Ozone-attributable asthma ED visits (older estimate)
subIndicators.value: ~10% of asthma ED visits citywide attributable to ozone in a 2011 DOHMH analysis; Staten Island, southern Brooklyn, central Queens, and the northwest Bronx had the highest ozone-related death rate estimates
subIndicators.source: NYC DOHMH (secondary citation, original analysis not independently re-fetched)

subIndicators.name: Citywide and Bronx child asthma ED visit rate, current
subIndicators.value: 143.7 per 10,000 children ages 5-17 citywide (2023); 239.8 per 10,000 in the Bronx (2023)
subIndicators.source: NYC Environment & Health Data Portal, neighborhood reports

subIndicators.name: Child asthma ED visit rate by borough, historical
subIndicators.value: Ages 5-17, 2016: Bronx 388.4 per 10,000 (highest); Manhattan 261.9; Brooklyn 188.2; Queens 128.1; Staten Island 81.8 (lowest); Citywide 217.1 per 10,000
subIndicators.source: NYC DOHMH, Epi Data Brief No. 126, 'Disparities among Children with Asthma in New York City'

subIndicators.name: June 2023 Canadian wildfire smoke episode
subIndicators.value: NYC's AQI peaked around 465 on June 7, 2023 (figures reported across sources range roughly 350-465 depending on monitor/averaging window); IQAir ranked NYC the world's worst major-city air quality that day. City officials called it the worst air quality since the 1960s. A materially smaller, ozone-driven Canadian wildfire smoke advisory recurred in mid-July 2026.
subIndicators.source: NYC Emergency Management press release (referencing the 2023 event) and CNBC/Fox Weather reporting

subIndicators.name: Local Law 43 / NYC Clean Heat — No. 6 and No. 4 residual heating oil phase-out
subIndicators.value: 100% of NYC buildings converted off No. 6 oil by the June 30, 2015 deadline (over 6,000 heating-system conversions, >75% to the cleanest fuel options); No. 4 oil phase-out deadline is January 1, 2030. Buildings burning No. 4/No. 6 oil were only ~1% of buildings but were responsible for an estimated 86% of citywide soot (PM2.5) from heating before the law.
subIndicators.source: NYC DEP / NYC Clean Heat program

subIndicators.name: Congestion pricing (Congestion Relief Zone) measured PM2.5 effect
subIndicators.value: In the first six months after the January 5, 2025 launch, average daily maximum PM2.5 in the Manhattan CBD/CRZ fell 22% (about 3.05 µg/m³ versus a modeled no-toll counterfactual of 13.8 µg/m³); the five-borough average fell 1.07 µg/m³ and the broader metro area 0.70 µg/m³. The weekly effect grew from 0.8 µg/m³ in week 1 to 4.9 µg/m³ by week 20, consistent with commuters shifting mode/route over time.
subIndicators.source: Cornell University study published in npj Clean Air (Dec 8, 2025), analyzing 42 regional air monitors Jan 2024-June 2025

global.levelRationale: NYC cannot unilaterally control two of the three largest pressures on its air-pollution ceiling: (1) upwind/interstate ozone-precursor transport, part of why the NY-NJ-CT region was reclassified from 'Moderate' to 'Serious' 2015-ozone-NAAQS nonattainment in July 2024 despite the city's own local control measures, and (2) increasingly frequent transboundary Canadian wildfire smoke (2023, recurring 2024 and again mid-July 2026) that is itself a downstream effect of global climate change. Layered on top, the Port of NY/NJ — the busiest port on the US East Coast — services NYC-area (and much wider) consumption demand and its ocean-going vessels alone account for 53% of the port's NOx and 36% of its PM2.5 emissions, a footprint driven by global containerized trade rather than by New Yorkers' local combustion. 'Needs attention' reflects a real, evidenced overshoot with only partial local leverage, not an unquantified hand-wave.
global.indicator: Transboundary/regional pollutant transport and Port of NY/NJ ocean-going vessel emissions
global.value: NY-NJ-CT ozone nonattainment area reclassified 'Serious' (2024); Port of NY/NJ ocean-going vessels = 53% of port NOx emissions and 36% of port PM2.5 emissions (2023 Port Emissions Inventory)
global.target: Clean Air Act attainment of the 2015 ozone NAAQS (70 ppb, 8-hour) for the NY-NJ-CT area; Port Authority's Clean Air Strategy / Clean Ports Program goals for zero-emission drayage and cargo-handling equipment
global.context: NYC's air-pollution footprint is not a closed local system. Regionally, the metro area's persistent ozone problem is driven substantially by NOx and VOC transport from upwind states and the wider Ozone Transport Region, which is why New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut jointly petitioned for and received the 2024 'Serious' reclassification rather than fixing it through city-level action alone — this is the ozone-pollution analogue to a 'consumption-based' emissions argument in the climate dimension. Separately, the Port of NY/NJ exists to serve import/export demand — much of it NYC consumption — and its ocean-going vessels, drayage trucks, and cargo-handling equipment emit PM2.5 and NOx concentrated in South Bronx, Red Hook, and New Jersey waterfront communities that host the region's port and last-mile e-commerce warehouse infrastructure. And the escalating frequency of Canadian wildfire smoke intrusions (2023, 2024, and again mid-July 2026) means an increasing share of NYC's worst PM2.5 days now originates entirely outside city and even national jurisdiction, tied to boreal-forest climate change. Aviation (JFK, LaGuardia, Newark) is a further plausible contributor to both local NOx/PM near the airports and to NYC's share of global aviation emissions, but no single quantified 'NYC aviation air-pollution footprint' figure was located in this research pass.
global.source: US EPA (ozone reclassification); Port Authority of NY/NJ, Clean Ports Report Card (2023 Port Emissions Inventory)
global.productionVsConsumption: mixed — transboundary transport (ozone precursors, wildfire smoke) is pollution NYC imports/receives regardless of its own emissions; Port of NY/NJ vessel/truck emissions are production-based emissions physically occurring in the harbor but generated in service of consumption demand (NYC's and the wider region's)

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 43 of 2010 / NYC Clean Heat
policyAnchors.relevance: Phased out the dirtiest heating oils (No. 6, then No. 4), the single most significant documented PM2.5 policy win in NYC air-quality history
policyAnchors.status2026: No. 6 oil phase-out has been at 100% compliance since 2015; No. 4 oil phase-out deadline is January 1, 2030 and is reportedly on track, though this research pass did not independently verify a current percent-remaining figure for No. 4 conversions

policyAnchors.name: Local Law 97 of 2019
policyAnchors.relevance: Building emissions caps reduce combustion (boilers, on-site fuel burning) that is also a PM2.5/NO2 source, so LL97 compliance carries direct air-quality co-benefits alongside its GHG purpose
policyAnchors.status2026: First compliance period (2024-2029): reportedly under 10% of covered buildings exceeded their cap based on 2024 performance; DOB began issuing the first Notices of Violation and penalties ($268/ton CO2e over the cap) around May 1, 2026. About 57% of buildings are projected to exceed the stricter 2030-2034 caps if no further retrofits occur.

policyAnchors.name: Congestion pricing / Central Business District Tolling Program
policyAnchors.relevance: Direct traffic-reduction air-quality intervention in and around the Manhattan core, with NYCCAS itself expanded specifically to measure it
policyAnchors.status2026: Launched January 5, 2025; DOHMH is running a legally required 2-year NYCCAS-based evaluation (baseline completed December 2024, initial findings report due 'early 2026' per NYS law) alongside independent academic measurement (Cornell, Dec 2025) already showing a 22% PM2.5 reduction in the tolling zone. The program has faced political/legal pushback from the Trump administration as of early 2026 reporting.

policyAnchors.name: NY-NJ-CT 2015 ozone NAAQS nonattainment reclassification
policyAnchors.relevance: The binding regulatory anchor for NYC's ozone/smog problem; 'Serious' status requires a tighter State Implementation Plan and controls
policyAnchors.status2026: Reclassified from Moderate to Serious effective per EPA's July 25, 2024 final rule after the area missed its August 3, 2024 attainment deadline for the 70 ppb standard

policyAnchors.name: Port Authority of NY/NJ Clean Air Strategy / Clean Ports Program
policyAnchors.relevance: The binding-ish operational framework (developed with EPA and stakeholders) for reducing truck, vessel, and cargo-handling emissions at the region's largest port, directly affecting South Bronx and NJ waterfront air quality
policyAnchors.status2026: Truck Replacement Program had retired 900+ older diesel trucks as of 2023; Port Authority received a large EPA Clean Ports grant (reported around $344 million) for electric cargo-handling equipment and drayage truck charging infrastructure; a proposed 'Green Drayage Accelerator' aims to move toward zero-emission drayage

actions: Sign up for NYC Emergency Management's Notify NYC alert system to get real-time air-quality/wildfire-smoke advisories, and pick up free KN95 masks at NYC public libraries during smoke events (as offered during the June 2023 and July 2026 Canadian wildfire smoke episodes).

If you own or sit on the board of a building burning No. 4 heating oil, start planning the conversion now — the Local Law 43 deadline is January 1, 2030 — using NYC's Retrofit Accelerator heating-oil-conversion resources.

If your building is covered by Local Law 97, check your building's emissions performance via NYC Accelerator/DOB and push your co-op or condo board to plan retrofits before the tighter 2030-2034 caps and escalating $268/ton penalties hit.

Support continuation of congestion pricing (the Congestion Relief Zone) given DOHMH/Cornell-measured PM2.5 reductions — the program has faced federal political pushback; contact your City Council member or testify at MTA/NYSDOT public comment sessions.

Push for zero-emission drayage and cargo-handling electrification at the Port of NY/NJ by engaging with the Port Authority's Clean Ports Program and groups like South Bronx Unite and the NYC Environmental Justice Alliance, given the South Bronx's outsized truck-traffic and asthma burden.

Use the NYC Environment & Health Data Portal's neighborhood reports (a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov) to check your own community district's PM2.5/asthma data and support community air-monitoring and advocacy groups such as WE ACT for Environmental Justice.
petalumaContrast: Petaluma's own draft portrait scores PM2.5 at 7.0-9.5 µg/m³ (2024, BAAQMD, level 30) — above the WHO guideline but meeting the federal NAAQS, with wildfire smoke as the dominant episodic driver for a small city with limited monitoring. NYC's author-computed citywide figure (~6.65 µg/m³, 2024) is comparable or even somewhat lower, but that single number masks a 2x intra-city gradient (5.3 to 10.5 µg/m³ across 59 monitored community districts) and a stark, quantified environmental-justice pattern — Bronx child asthma ED visit rates roughly 1.7-2x the citywide rate and historically up to 4-5x Staten Island's — that a 60,000-person city with one regional monitoring network cannot show at anywhere near this resolution. NYC's dominant sources (traffic, building combustion, port/truck freight) and levers (Local Law 43/97, congestion pricing) are also structurally different from Petaluma's wildfire-and-agriculture-dominated exposure.
dataGaps: No single official DOHMH-published 'citywide' PM2.5 headline figure was located; the value used here is an unweighted mean the author computed across all 59 NYCCAS community districts from Appendix 3 of the DOHMH report. DOHMH's Environment & Health Data Portal data-explorer tool is interactive/JavaScript-based and could not be scraped directly for an official aggregate — someone with portal access or the underlying dataset (data.cityofnewyork.us) should confirm whether a population-weighted citywide figure exists and differs materially from this unweighted estimate.

Current-year (2023-2025) asthma ED visit rates broken out for Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island individually were not found; only citywide (143.7 per 10,000, 2023) and Bronx (239.8 per 10,000, 2023) figures were located via the EH Data Portal neighborhood report. The full five-borough table used here (388.4 Bronx / 261.9 Manhattan / 188.2 Brooklyn / 128.1 Queens / 81.8 Staten Island) is from 2016. NYS DOH EpiQuery or DOHMH's asthma dashboard would have the current equivalent.

NYCCAS's ozone metric is a 'summertime average,' not the EPA regulatory 8-hour design value used for NAAQS attainment/nonattainment determinations; the actual current design value for the NY-NJ-CT area was not independently fetched in this pass.

No quantified figure for aviation-attributable local air pollution near JFK/LaGuardia/Newark, or for NYC's share of global aviation emissions, was located. Port Authority of NY/NJ or FAA environmental/sustainability reports would have this.

DOHMH's own legally required 2-year NYCCAS evaluation of congestion pricing's air-quality effect (baseline completed December 2024, report due 'early 2026') was referenced in a 2025 press release but its actual findings report was not locatable/fetched — it may not yet be published as of this research pass.

Should these be labeled 'confidence: medium' as I did, or lower, given they are a derived secondary calculation on top of a primary source rather than a directly published number?
